verdicts.threatModel: Build-time supply chain only. The attacker must control the upstream publisher or its hosting: the AppImage/appimagetool GitHub `continuous` release asset (packaging/linux/package.sh:113) or the nuget.org package Microsoft.Trusted.Signing.Client (packaging/windows/sign.ps1:77). Transport is HTTPS (curl -fsSL to github.com; Invoke-WebRequest to https://www.nuget.org), so a network-position attacker cannot substitute content; no Ember user, file, or runtime input reaches either URL.
verdicts.reachability: Both downloads run only in release packaging. package.sh fetches appimagetool when neither APPIMAGETOOL nor an appimagetool on PATH exists and the cached copy is absent (lines 109-116); release.yml:223 runs it on ubuntu-22.04 runners that do not preinstall appimagetool, so it executes on every Linux release. sign.ps1 downloads the NuGet package only on the Azure Trusted Signing branch (lines 72-89), reached from package.ps1 in release.yml:158-171 when the AZURE_* secrets are set and WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE is not. Neither URL pins a version or digest: `continuous` is a mutable tag and the NuGet URL omits a version, resolving to latest.
verdicts.impact: No end-user attack surface. If upstream were compromised, the downloaded tool would execute in the release job: the appimagetool binary builds and embeds the runtime into the shipped AppImage (tampered release artifact), and the Azure dlib is loaded by signtool with AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET in the environment (credential exposure, signing of attacker content). Severity is bounded by needing a publisher-level compromise; the gap is missing pinning/hash verification, not an exploitable flaw reachable by an external attacker today. Missing pinning also makes release builds non-reproducible.
verdicts.rationale: Both cluster members are real unpinned, unhashed fetches of executable build tooling (package.sh:113 mutable `continuous` asset; sign.ps1:77 unversioned NuGet package), confirmed reachable from release.yml. Devil's advocate: HTTPS to first-party hosts, GitHub-hosted ephemeral runners, and the post-sign `signtool verify /pa` (sign.ps1:91) remove MITM and detect unsigned output, but do not detect a malicious upstream tool. No attacker-controlled source exists short of upstream compromise, so this is a supply-chain hardening gap (pin appimagetool to a tagged release with sha256; pin the NuGet package version and verify its hash), not a TRUE_POSITIVE.
